title: Bridge Mode Fallback & Capacity Warmup — Runbook Draft
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working draft for an operational path we call 'bridge mode' — a minimal-quality, high-reliability fallback used during infra incidents where GPU-backed inference loses capacity (node failure, driver/kernel corruption, or physical GPU replacement). Bridge mode aims to keep customer-facing endpoints up with higher latency / lower throughput rather than full outage while we perform replacements, cordon/drain, or capacity injection.

Audience:
- Primary: on-call SREs and infra engineers performing node maintenance and emergency recovery.
- Secondary: serving-runtime engineers, support, and incident commanders during escalations.

Assumptions and constraints (read before action):
- Bridge mode relies on a small number of CPU-only replicas (or quantized small-GPU variants) already staged per regional pool. If not present, follow the 'warmup' steps below.
- Clients can tolerate increased latency and a token cost delta during fallback; we must notify major customers via the status page when SLOs degrade beyond thresholds.
- For safety we prefer rolling, targeted actions; avoid broad cluster-wide cordon/drain unless absolutely necessary.

Quick decision checklist (yes/no):
- Is the incident causing >30% capacity loss in a region? If yes, continue.
- Are auto-retries failing or queueing for >60s on average? If yes, bridge mode recommended.
- Is there a known driver/kernel bug or hardware failure? If yes, prepare for GPU replacement.

Bridge mode activation (fast path):
1) Announce on #oncall and incident channel with subject: "Bridge mode ON — <region> — <short reason>". Include IM/phone pager for primary infra.
2) Flip routing policy for affected routes to: priority = [dedicated-warmup, cpu-fallback, remote-region], maintain read-only status for non-critical routes.
   - Commands: internal CLI: redwood route update --route <route> --policy fallback:cpu,priority=1
   - If using traffic-shaper: set max concurrency lower bound for fallback routes.
3) Scale up CPU fallback replicas:
   - kubectl -n inference scale deploy/cpu-fallback --replicas=5 --context=<cluster>
   - If using autoscaler, set minReplicas=3 temporarily (make sure to revert).
4) Reduce aggressive batching to lower tail-latency for degraded path: edit ConfigMap inference-batching (reduce max_batch=8, max_wait_ms=20).
5) Disable non-essential background work (evals, heavy warmup pipelines) to free resources in cluster.
6) Observe metrics for 10 minutes: token throughput, tail latency (p95/p99), queue depth. If unstable, escalate to on-call infra lead.

GPU replacement / physical node path (summary):
- If node health indicates hardware fault (SMART errors, ECC, NVML driver errors), follow hardware swap flow: notify data center ops, mark node for physical replacement.
- Steps to prepare node for removal:
   a) cordon node: kubectl cordon <node>
   b) graceful drain with pod eviction/annotation: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=15m
   c) watch for stuck pods: kubectl describe pod <pod> -n inference; if stuck on terminating >10m, escalate and consider force-delete after confirming state.
- After physical GPU install, run acceptance: nvml-smi-check.sh -> run model-canary-suite for 10 chains at target seq len.
- If kernel/driver previously implicated, rotate drivers after maintenance using controlled rollout: node selector label drivers:v2 -> patch daemonset -> roll restart.

Cordon/Drain nuances (lessons learned):
- Do NOT cordon indiscriminately. If you cannot warmup fallback capacity in 5 minutes, cordon only 1 node at a time and monitor queue depth.
- Some stateful auxiliary pods (cache priming, metrics exporters) can lock eviction for >10m; check EvictionPolicy annotations and reduce dependencies.
- Force-deleting inference pods can cause KV cache loss and increased downstream latency for ~10–20m. Consider prefilling incremental cache on fallback replicas.

Capacity warmup checklist (when rapid capacity add needed):
- Warmup image warming: pull images in parallel to avoid startup storms. Example: kubectl get nodes -o name | xargs -n1 -P10 -I% kubectl --context=<cluster> exec % -- crictl pull <image>
- Use warmup runner job to pre-run 1 inference request per new replica to populate KV caches. job: inference-warmup-job (runs 2x per replica).
- Monitor cost and token usage and annotate scaling action in the incident timeline.

Verification and rollback criteria:
- Success: p95 latency within 2x of baseline AND error rate <2% for 20 consecutive minutes after route flip.
- Partial success: p95 >2x but system steady; communicate degraded SLOs and continue with hardware replacement schedule.
- Failure: queue depth trending up or error rate increasing — revert routing change (route update --route <route> --policy primary) and investigate root cause deeper.

Escalation path:
- On-call SRE -> Infra lead -> Serving runtime lead -> Engineering manager. Use phone/pager after 15m of unresolved degradation.
- If incident impacts >10% of customers or SLA breach imminent, declare P1 and bring in support and product comms.

Post-incident / Postmortem items (to capture in timeline):
- Time of detection, time bridge mode enabled, nodes cordoned, hardware replaced, warmup started, final recovery.
- Actor names and commands used (copy-paste of critical commands used).
- Attach logs: nvml logs, kubelet logs for affected nodes, route-change audit.
- Followups: ensure we have at least 2 warmup replicas per region, add an automated warning when node driver errors exceed threshold, create a test that simulates eviction storm in staging.

Open questions / TODOs (notes-to-self):
- We should document and automate the exact route flip CLI (current CLI is brittle). TODO: create redwood infra cli task (JIRA-OPS-7399).
- Decide default CPU fallback image size — current debate: quantized-3B vs cpu-1B. Marco prefers 3B for quality, Sasha prefers 1B for cost. Put for architecture review.
- Add an automated pre-warm step that runs whenever a node enters NotReady for >30s.

Quick reference commands (common):
- Cordon: kubectl cordon <node>
- Drain: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
- Uncordon: kubectl uncordon <node>
- Scale fallback: kubectl -n inference scale deploy/cpu-fallback --replicas=<n>
- View pods on node: kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node> -n inference

Appendix A — Sample incident timeline (example):
- 09:03 Detection: autoscaler alerts on GpuUtil spike and eviction notices.
- 09:07 Bridge mode ON: scaled cpu-fallback to 5, routing flipped, brief announcement.
- 09:15 Cordon node ip-10-0-32-12, drain started.
- 09:34 Pod stuck on terminating, force-evicted after 4x10s checks.
- 09:50 Hardware team replaced GPU, drivers upgraded, acceptance passed.
- 10:05 Gradual uncordon and revert routing, p95 returned to baseline by 10:18.

Appendix B — Useful links and references:
- Confluence: infra/fallback-arch-2024
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/458
- Warmup job manifest: k8s/inference/warmup-job.yaml (internal repo)

Endnotes:
- This is intentionally a lightweight, operational-first draft. It should be tested in the next SRE game day (Q1) and refined into a canonical runbook if it proves effective.

Notes to self (informal):
- Remember to add snippet for autoscaler annotation change and provide exact CLI aliases to avoid typos.
- Consider pre-seeding Prometheus alert with a dedicated bridge-mode alert so oncall doesn't have to interpret multiple signals at once.
- Remove these NOTES before promoting to 'final'.
